title: Work as offering
hookLine: Herbert's sweeping makes drudgery divine; Krishna tells Arjuna to offer whatever he does
tomorrow: what did an emperor learn from a beehive?

lines: A STONE THAT TURNS THINGS TO GOLD.
WHO SWEEPS A ROOM AS FOR THY LAWS.
cards: Somebody has to clean the spreadsheet, empty the office dishwasher, file the receipts.
The English poet George Herbert wrote a poem about that kind of work and called it The Elixir, after the alchemists' dream of a stone that turns whatever it touches to gold.
His stone is a small phrase: for thy sake, done for God. "A servant with this clause / Makes drudgery divine: / Who sweeps a room as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine."
And he ends: "This is the well-known stone / That turneth all to gold."

teach.b: Notice Herbert still calls it drudgery. The room doesn't stop being a room, and the broom doesn't get lighter. What changes is who it's for.

Nothing is so lowly, the poem says, that it won't grow bright and clean when it's done for God's sake. Herbert writes as a Christian at prayer, and the poem opens by asking God to teach him to see him in all things.
A neighbor tradition makes the same move on a battlefield.

teach.h: WHATEVER YOU DO, DO IT AS AN OFFERING.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, whatever discipline you keep, do it as an offering to me.

teach.h: KARMA YOGA: THE PATH OF ACTION.
teach.b: The Gita calls this way karma yoga, the path of action, and the Gita gives it a sharp edge: your right is to the work, never to its fruits.

teach.h: YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK, NOT ITS FRUITS.
teach.b: So the offering isn't a mood you have to summon. It changes what the task is for. The spreadsheet stops being proof that you're stuck.
It becomes something given. Herbert's thy and Krishna's me aren't the same address, and each tradition gives its own reasons.
But both teach this with the hands: the dull task, offered, is no longer only dull.

how: Christians who pray the way Herbert's poem does offer ordinary work to God; Hindus following the Gita's karma yoga dedicate their actions to God without clinging to the results.

o: doing a task for something beyond yourself, not the reward
working without pay as a volunteer on weekends
giving your paycheck away to a religious community

games.q: the stone and the offering: tap the pairs.
p: Herbert's poem of the golden stone
what the Gita says isn't your right

s: work as offering means pretending boring work is fun
Herbert still calls it drudgery. the offering changes who it's for, not how it feels.
in the Gita, Krishna says to offer even your eating
whatever you do, eat, offer or give: do it as an offering.
the Gita promises good results if you offer your work
it says the opposite: your right is to the work, never to its fruits.

games.q: your cousin stacks chairs after every event at her community hall and says it's pointless. what would Herbert's poem tell her?
o: do it as for God, and the stacking itself becomes something offered.
stack them fast so she has more time for the parts that matter.
only the work done during the service itself counts as offered.
games.why: who sweeps a room as for thy laws makes that and th' action fine. the chairs are the room.

practice: Choose the one task this week you'd most like to skip. Say quietly, out loud, who you'd offer it to: God, if you pray, or the people it will serve, if you don't. Then sit with that task in mind, offered, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Work as offering: the dull task done for someone, not for its fruits. Herbert's swept room, the Gita's offering.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the path of action, work offered without grasping at its fruits.

carryVoice: Something to keep: offered, Herbert's well-known stone, small enough to fit in a dustpan. That's the work week, offered.
